_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning about why people work and how work benefits both individuals and their communities.

toLevel2.question: People work to earn income, find purpose, and connect with others through what they do.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Income, purpose, and connection are common reasons people work, beyond just earning money.

distractors.explanation: Work fills more than one role at once: it pays bills, gives meaning, and links workers to others.

toLevel2.question: Paid work is the only kind of work that has any value to a community.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Unpaid work such as parenting, caring, and volunteering has real value even though no money is paid.

distractors.explanation: Treating only paid work as valuable ignores the unpaid work that keeps families and communities running.

toLevel2.question: Volunteer work is unpaid work that someone does to help others or support the community.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Volunteers freely give time and effort to help others, without expecting payment in return.

distractors.explanation: Volunteering is widely understood as unpaid help offered to community organisations or causes.

toLevel2.question: Essential workers include nurses, teachers, and farmers who support the community in different ways.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Nurses, teachers, and farmers each provide services or goods that the wider community depends on.

distractors.explanation: These three roles are commonly listed as essential because their work supports everyone's wellbeing.

toLevel2.question: Parenting and caring for family members is not work because no money changes hands.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Parenting and caring are real work; they involve real time, skill, and effort, even when unpaid.

distractors.explanation: Defining work only by payment misses the unpaid work that supports families and communities every day.

toLevel2.question: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have continued knowledge systems that have sustained communities for many thousands of years.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: First Nations knowledge systems for managing Country, food, and trade have continued across many thousands of years.

distractors.explanation: This ongoing knowledge is well documented and continues to support communities today, not only in the past.

toLevel2.question: Different types of work in a community include only paid jobs, with no unpaid or volunteer roles.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Communities rely on paid, unpaid, and volunteer work, all of which contribute to wellbeing.

distractors.explanation: Reducing community work to paid jobs alone misses the substantial unpaid and volunteer contributions.

toLevel2.question: A nurse and a teacher do completely different work and never share any common features at any time.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Both nursing and teaching are care-focused work that supports the wellbeing of others, so they share clear common features.

distractors.explanation: Treating these roles as completely separate misses the shared focus on supporting the wellbeing of others.

toLevel2.question: All workers in a community must do exactly the same job for the community to function well.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Communities function because many different workers do many different jobs that complement each other.

distractors.explanation: Treating one job as enough ignores the wide range of work that keeps a community running.

toLevel2.question: A volunteer who coaches a junior sports team is doing work that benefits the community.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Volunteer coaching benefits players, families, and the wider community, even though it is unpaid.

distractors.explanation: Volunteer coaching is one common example of unpaid work that benefits a community.

toLevel2.question: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander economies in the past included no organised work of any kind.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: First Nations economies included organised work: managing Country, harvesting food, building tools, and maintaining trade.

distractors.explanation: Treating these economies as having no organised work ignores documented systems of land management, harvest, and trade.

toLevel2.question: Every local area in Australia has the same types of common work regardless of its resources or needs.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Different areas have different common work, shaped by their land, resources, and community needs.

distractors.explanation: Treating local work as uniform across Australia ignores how regions differ in resources, industries, and needs.

toLevel2.question: Why do people work?
toLevel2.correct: To earn income, find purpose, and connect with others
toLevel2.correctExplanation: People work for many reasons including income, purpose, and connection.

distractors.answer: To avoid every kind of activity outside the home
distractors.explanation: Avoiding all activity is the opposite of going to work each day.

distractors.answer: To stop other people from doing similar work
distractors.explanation: Most workers do not work to block others from working in similar roles.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes volunteer work?
toLevel2.correct: Unpaid work done to help others or support the community
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Volunteer work is unpaid work freely given to help others or support a community.

distractors.answer: Paid work that always pays double the usual rate of pay
distractors.explanation: Volunteering is unpaid, not double-paid.

distractors.answer: Work that no person ever chooses to do for any reason
distractors.explanation: Many people choose to volunteer; it is widely chosen, not avoided by all.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is an example of unpaid work?
toLevel2.correct: Caring for a younger sibling without receiving any money
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Caring for a younger sibling is unpaid work that contributes to the family.

distractors.answer: Selling lemonade for cash at a community market stall
distractors.explanation: Selling lemonade for cash is paid work, not unpaid work.

distractors.answer: Working as a paid weekend assistant at a cafe in town
distractors.explanation: A paid cafe assistant role is paid work, not unpaid work.

toLevel2.question: Which group is most often described as essential workers in a community?
toLevel2.correct: Nurses, teachers, and farmers who support everyone's wellbeing
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Nurses, teachers, and farmers are commonly described as essential workers.

distractors.answer: Children, retirees, and pets who live in the community quietly
distractors.explanation: Children, retirees, and pets are valued community members but are not described as essential workers.

distractors.answer: Tourists who visit the community for short holiday breaks
distractors.explanation: Tourists are short-term visitors, not workers who keep the community running.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is a benefit of work for an individual?
toLevel2.correct: Income, purpose, and connection through what they do
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Work provides income, purpose, and connection at the individual level.

distractors.answer: An immediate reduction in every community service available
distractors.explanation: Work does not reduce community services; many services depend on workers.

distractors.answer: A guarantee that they will never need to learn anything new
distractors.explanation: Most work involves ongoing learning rather than ending it.

toLevel2.question: Which list includes only types of work?
toLevel2.correct: Paid, unpaid, and volunteer work in a local community
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Paid, unpaid, and volunteer work are the three main categories of work in a community.

distractors.answer: A computer game, a movie, and a packet of biscuits
distractors.explanation: These items are entertainment products, not types of work.

distractors.answer: A football, a basketball, and a tennis racquet at a shop
distractors.explanation: These items are sporting equipment, not types of work.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander economies that have continued for thousands of years?
toLevel2.correct: Organised systems of work that managed Country, food, and trade
toLevel2.correctExplanation: First Nations economies are documented as organised systems of work for managing Country, food, and trade.

distractors.answer: Random activity with no planning or shared knowledge across communities
distractors.explanation: These economies are well documented as planned, not random.

distractors.answer: A single shared system used identically by every nation across Australia
distractors.explanation: Different nations have always had distinct knowledge systems and practices, not a single shared one.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is most likely an example of paid work?
toLevel2.correct: A baker who sells bread at a shop for a wage each week
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A baker who is paid for selling bread is doing paid work.

distractors.answer: A neighbour who waters a friend's plants once for free
distractors.explanation: Watering a friend's plants without payment is unpaid help, not paid work.

distractors.answer: A student who helps an elderly relative with shopping unpaid
distractors.explanation: Helping an unpaid relative with shopping is unpaid work, not paid work.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best illustrates the link between work and community wellbeing?
toLevel2.correct: Nurses, teachers, and farmers each support different parts of community life
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Workers in different roles each support different parts of community life.

distractors.answer: Workers always weaken community life by doing different kinds of jobs
distractors.explanation: Workers strengthen community life rather than weakening it.

distractors.answer: Workers have no link to community wellbeing in any community
distractors.explanation: Workers are clearly linked to community wellbeing through the services and goods they provide.

toLevel2.question: Which scenario best shows the value of unpaid work?
toLevel2.correct: A parent prepares meals and cares for a young child every day at home
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Daily caring and meal preparation is unpaid work that supports the family every day.

distractors.answer: A parent spends every day at home doing nothing for the family
distractors.explanation: Doing nothing for the family is not work and is not what most parents do.

distractors.answer: A parent ignores the needs of every child in the household at home
distractors.explanation: Ignoring household needs is not work; it is the absence of work.

toLevel2.question: First Nations rangers care for Country today using knowledge built over thousands of years. Which one of the following best describes this work?
toLevel2.correct: A continuing tradition of organised work that supports both Country and community wellbeing
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Ranger work continues long-standing traditions of caring for Country and supports community wellbeing.

distractors.answer: A new activity invented in the past few years with no connection to earlier knowledge systems
distractors.explanation: Caring for Country has continued for many thousands of years and is not a recent invention.

distractors.answer: A short-term private hobby that has no connection to community wellbeing
distractors.explanation: Ranger work is organised paid or community-supported work, not a private hobby.

toLevel2.question: Why might one local area have a different mix of common work from another local area?
toLevel2.correct: Different areas have different needs, resources, and industries that shape work
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Different needs, resources, and industries shape what work is common in different areas.

distractors.answer: Every area in Australia has the same mix of work in exactly the same proportions
distractors.explanation: Different areas have very different mixes of work, depending on local conditions.

distractors.answer: Local areas decide their work mix only by what was common 100 years ago
distractors.explanation: Local work patterns change over time based on current needs and resources, not only the past.

toLevel2.sentence: People work for many reasons, including {{blank:1}} that pays for daily life and a sense of {{blank:2}} that helps them feel their work matters.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not what work pays.
Fixture is a scheduled match, not what work pays.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniformity is the state of being the same, not a feeling work can give.
Scoring is recording points in a match, not a feeling work can give.

toLevel2.sentence: Three common types of work in a community are {{blank:1}} work, unpaid work such as caring at home, and {{blank:2}} work freely given to help others.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniformed describes clothing, not a category of work.
Scored describes a competition outcome, not a category of work.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniformed describes clothing, not a category of work.
Fixture is a scheduled match, not a category of work.

toLevel3.question: A community member who volunteers each week at a local food bank is not really doing work because no payment is received.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Volunteering is real work even when unpaid; it provides time, skill, and effort that meet real community needs.

distractors.explanation: Treating volunteer help as not-real-work misses the substantial contribution unpaid work makes to communities.

toLevel3.question: Paid and unpaid work both contribute to the wellbeing of a community in real ways.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Communities rely on a mix of paid and unpaid work to function well.

distractors.explanation: Both paid and unpaid work add to community wellbeing; one cannot replace the other.

toLevel3.question: If everyone stopped doing unpaid work tomorrow, communities would still function exactly the same as before.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Unpaid work — parenting, caring, volunteering — is a major part of how communities function.

distractors.explanation: Removing unpaid work would leave many community needs unmet, since unpaid work is widespread.

toLevel3.question: First Nations economies before colonisation had complex work systems for fishing, hunting, and managing Country.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Documented work systems included fish traps, hunting practices, fire management, and seasonal harvesting.

distractors.explanation: These work systems are well documented in archaeological and historical records and supported communities for many thousands of years.

toLevel3.question: A teacher contributes to the community only through their pay, not through the skills they pass on to students.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Teachers contribute through both their work and the skills, knowledge, and confidence they pass on to students.

distractors.explanation: Treating contribution as pay-only ignores the long-term effect teachers have on students and communities.

toLevel3.question: People only choose work for the money it pays; purpose and connection have no real role in any work choice.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Many workers choose work for income alongside purpose, connection, and identity. Money is not the only reason.

distractors.explanation: Treating money as the only reason for choosing work misses the role of purpose and connection for many workers.

toLevel3.question: First Nations rangers who care for Country today continue traditions of work that have existed for thousands of years.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Caring for Country has been organised work for thousands of years and continues through ranger and land-care programs today.

distractors.explanation: First Nations ranger and land-care programs continue traditions of work that have always supported communities.

toLevel3.question: If a community had no farmers, getting locally grown fresh food would not be affected in any way.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Without farmers, locally grown fresh food would become much harder to get and supply chains would change.

distractors.explanation: Treating farming as separable from food supply ignores how directly farmer work affects what reaches local shops.

toLevel3.question: A community member spends weekends coaching a junior sports team for free. Which type of work is this?
toLevel3.correct: Volunteer work that benefits the team and the wider community
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Coaching a junior team for free is volunteer work that benefits the team and the community.

distractors.answer: Paid professional work usually done by senior coaches each weekend
distractors.explanation: Unpaid coaching is volunteer work, not paid professional work.

distractors.answer: Work that has no connection to the wellbeing of any community
distractors.explanation: Volunteer coaching clearly supports community wellbeing through sport and connection.

toLevel3.question: If everyone in a town stopped doing unpaid work tomorrow, what is the most likely outcome for the town?
toLevel3.correct: Many community needs would be unmet because unpaid work supports daily life
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Unpaid work — caring, parenting, volunteering — supports daily life in many communities.

distractors.answer: The town would continue exactly the same because only paid work has any effect
distractors.explanation: Unpaid work is a major part of how communities function; removing it has real effects.

distractors.answer: Every paid worker would suddenly stop their work for the rest of the week
distractors.explanation: Stopping unpaid work would not by itself stop paid workers in a town from working.

toLevel3.question: A young person interviews a local farmer about her work. Which idea best explains why farming is described as essential work?
toLevel3.correct: Farming produces the food that the community depends on every single day for meals
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Farming is essential because it produces food that communities depend on every day.

distractors.answer: Farming has no connection to the community because food appears on shelves anyway
distractors.explanation: Food on shelves comes from farmers; treating food supply as automatic ignores their work.

distractors.answer: Farming is mostly a private hobby that does not affect any community member's wellbeing
distractors.explanation: Most farming is paid work that supplies a community, not a private hobby.

toLevel3.question: Which scenario best illustrates the value of unpaid work in a community?
toLevel3.correct: A grandparent looks after grandchildren so a parent can do paid work each day
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Caring for grandchildren is unpaid work that enables paid work and supports the family.

distractors.answer: A grandparent never sees grandchildren and contributes nothing to the family at all
distractors.explanation: Family connection and unpaid care are valuable contributions to community wellbeing.

distractors.answer: A grandparent only buys gifts for the family and does no other unpaid work
distractors.explanation: Buying gifts is one form of contribution, but daily unpaid care work is also significant.

toLevel3.question: A First Nations community has fish traps that have been used for thousands of years. Which idea best describes the work involved?
toLevel3.correct: Organised work that combines knowledge of Country, water, and fish behaviour over generations
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Fish traps reflect organised work using detailed knowledge of Country, water, and fish behaviour.

distractors.answer: Random activity with no planning, knowledge, or shared methods between people
distractors.explanation: These systems are highly organised and use shared knowledge passed across generations.

distractors.answer: Work that has no link to economic activity at any time in any community
distractors.explanation: Fish-trap work has long supported communities economically through food and trade.

toLevel3.question: Which one of the following best illustrates how work can give a person purpose?
toLevel3.correct: A nurse who feels her work helps people recover from illness in the community
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A nurse who feels her work supports recovery is finding purpose through her role.

distractors.answer: A nurse who feels nothing about her work or its effect on patients in the ward
distractors.explanation: Most workers feel some connection to their work, especially in care-focused roles.

distractors.answer: A nurse who has no patients and never sees any community member at work
distractors.explanation: Most nurses interact with patients and the community as part of their daily work.

toLevel3.question: Why are different occupations valuable in a community?
toLevel3.correct: Each occupation contributes a different service or product that others depend on
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Different occupations contribute different services and products that the community needs.

distractors.answer: Each occupation produces exactly the same product as every other occupation
distractors.explanation: Different occupations produce different things, not the same product.

distractors.answer: Each occupation has no link to anyone else's daily wellbeing in the community
distractors.explanation: Most occupations are clearly linked to community wellbeing through their work.

toLevel3.question: Which one of the following is the best example of paid work that supports the community?
toLevel3.correct: A bus driver who transports students to school each weekday morning
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A bus driver who takes students to school is doing paid work that supports the community.

distractors.answer: A bus driver who refuses to drive any student to school at any time
distractors.explanation: Refusing to drive students would not support the community.

distractors.answer: A bus driver who never takes any work in the community
distractors.explanation: A driver who takes no work is not doing paid work that supports the community.

toLevel3.question: Which scenario best illustrates First Nations economies in continuing knowledge systems?
toLevel3.correct: Aboriginal rangers using fire knowledge to manage Country today as part of their daily work
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Aboriginal ranger and land-management programs apply fire knowledge today as part of organised work.

distractors.answer: Aboriginal communities never using fire knowledge in any way for any purpose at any time
distractors.explanation: Fire management has long been used and continues today through ranger programs.

distractors.answer: Aboriginal communities only using fire knowledge in stories without any current work
distractors.explanation: Fire knowledge is applied in current land management work, not only in stories.

toLevel3.question: Which one of the following best illustrates the link between work and community connection?
toLevel3.correct: A baker who knows local customers by name and supports a school fundraiser
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A baker connecting with customers and supporting a fundraiser is building community connection.

distractors.answer: A baker who refuses to interact with any local customer at any time
distractors.explanation: Refusing all customer contact is the opposite of building connection.

distractors.answer: A baker who has no customers and produces no goods at any time
distractors.explanation: A baker who has no customers is not connecting with anyone through their work.

toLevel3.question: Why might a regional town have more farming work than a city centre?
toLevel3.correct: The town has more farmland and rural conditions that support agricultural work
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Farming work follows farmland and rural conditions, which are more common in regional towns.

distractors.answer: Every town and city in Australia has exactly the same amount of farming work
distractors.explanation: Farming work varies widely between regional and urban areas.

distractors.answer: Cities always have more farming work than regional towns under all conditions
distractors.explanation: Cities typically have less, not more, farming work than regional towns.

toLevel3.question: Which scenario best illustrates a worker contributing both income and skills to their family?
toLevel3.correct: A parent earns wages and also teaches a child how to read and cook each week
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Earning wages and teaching a child new skills are two different contributions to the family.

distractors.answer: A parent earns wages but refuses to teach the child anything outside of school
distractors.explanation: Most parents teach their children outside of school as part of family life.

distractors.answer: A parent earns no wages and never teaches the child any new skill at home
distractors.explanation: This option misses both contributions, not just one.

toLevel3.sentence: First Nations rangers care for {{blank:1}} today using knowledge built over many thousands of years; this is paid {{blank:2}} that continues a long tradition.

distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not what rangers care for.
Fixture is a scheduled match, not what rangers care for.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not what rangers do as a paid role.
Season is a period of competition, not what rangers do as a paid role.

toLevel4.question: Mia interviews her grandmother, who volunteers at the community garden; the interview shows how unpaid work can support a community.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Volunteer garden work provides shared food, social connection, and care for community spaces.

distractors.explanation: Unpaid garden work is one example of how volunteers contribute substantially to a community.

toLevel4.question: Jarrah reads about Yolngu people using detailed knowledge of tides for fishing; this work has no link to economic activity.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Fishing organised around tide knowledge has long been an economic activity that feeds communities and supports trade.

distractors.explanation: Treating culturally informed fishing as outside economic activity ignores how it has supported communities for many thousands of years.

toLevel4.question: Mia interviews her grandmother, who volunteers each week at a community garden. Which idea best describes the grandmother's work?
toLevel4.correct: Volunteer work that supports community wellbeing through shared food and connection
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Volunteering at a community garden is unpaid work that supports community wellbeing.

distractors.answer: Paid professional work usually done by full-time gardeners across the community
distractors.explanation: Volunteering is unpaid, not full-time professional work.

distractors.answer: Work that has no link to community wellbeing of any kind in any town
distractors.explanation: Community garden work clearly contributes to community wellbeing.

toLevel4.question: Jarrah reads about Yolngu people using detailed knowledge of tides for fishing. Which idea best describes this work?
toLevel4.correct: Organised economic activity using detailed knowledge of Country and water for food and trade
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Tide-based fishing has long been organised economic activity that fed communities and supported trade.

distractors.answer: Random activity with no planning, knowledge, or community benefit at any stage
distractors.explanation: These systems are highly organised and use detailed shared knowledge.

distractors.answer: Work that exists only in stories and never sustained any community across thousands of years
distractors.explanation: Tide-based fishing has sustained communities for many thousands of years and continues today.

toLevel4.question: Anika lists the work that supports her local hospital. Which list best fits the topic?
toLevel4.correct: Doctors, nurses, cleaners, and volunteers who all contribute to patient wellbeing
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Hospitals depend on a mix of paid medical staff, support staff, and volunteers to function well.

distractors.answer: Tourists, customers, and visitors who walk past the hospital each weekend
distractors.explanation: Tourists and visitors do not provide the work that supports a hospital.

distractors.answer: Actors, musicians, and athletes who perform in stadiums far from the hospital
distractors.explanation: Performers are not the workers who support a hospital each day.

toLevel4.question: Sam discovers that his neighbour does paid work as a paramedic and unpaid work raising her own children. Which idea best fits these activities?
toLevel4.correct: Both paid work and unpaid work contribute to community wellbeing in different ways
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Paid and unpaid work each contribute to community wellbeing in different ways.

distractors.answer: Only paid work counts as work that contributes to a community in any way
distractors.explanation: Both kinds of work are recognised as contributing to community wellbeing.

distractors.answer: Unpaid work is harmful to a community when it is combined with paid work
distractors.explanation: Combining paid work and unpaid family care is widespread and beneficial, not harmful.

toLevel4.question: Lila visits a regional town and notices many farms. Which idea best explains why farming is more common there than in a city centre?
toLevel4.correct: The town has more farmland and rural conditions that support agricultural work
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Farming is more common where farmland and rural conditions support agricultural work.

distractors.answer: Every town and city has exactly the same amount of farming work in any year
distractors.explanation: Farming work varies widely across local areas, depending on conditions.

distractors.answer: Cities always have more farming work than any regional town in Australia
distractors.explanation: Cities typically have far less farming work than regional towns.

toLevel4.question: Kofi reads about a First Nations ranger program that combines caring for Country with paid work. Which idea best fits this program?
toLevel4.correct: Paid work that continues long-standing knowledge systems of caring for Country
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Ranger programs continue long-standing knowledge systems and are organised paid work that supports communities.

distractors.answer: A new activity with no link to long-standing knowledge of Country at all
distractors.explanation: Caring for Country has continued across many thousands of years.

distractors.answer: Unpaid hobby work that has no connection to community wellbeing in the region
